title: The Consumerization of Health Care: How Patients Are Reshaping the Industry
gist: BCG's 2026 survey of 9,914 consumers in ten countries finds health care increasingly judged like a consumer service — ~2/3 want more control over treatments and costs, >60% expect retail-level convenience — strongest in China, India, the UAE and Brazil and among millennials and higher-income groups (48% willing to self-pay for GLP-1s); BCG expects consumerization to keep advancing in self-manageable categories but never become complete, with biopharma, medtech, providers and payers needing consumer-grade experiences, LLM discoverability and new pricing.

insights.claim: In BCG's 2026 survey of 9,914 consumers across ten markets, almost half said health care products are just another consumer good, roughly two in three want more control over treatment choices and costs, and more than 60% expect retail-store convenience from health care.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Demand-side shift favors direct-to-consumer health models and consumer-grade service providers.
insights.locator: Are health care products just another consumer good

insights.claim: Consumers are proactively seeking specific treatments — GLP-1 weight-loss drugs like Mounjaro and Wegovy, sexual-health medicines like Cialis and Viagra, aesthetics like Botox, and blood-pressure and glucose monitors — evidencing health care consumerization in practice.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Lifestyle-adjacent, self-pay categories are where consumer brands and DTC channels capture the most value.
insights.locator: More and more, consumers want information

insights.claim: BCG built a 0–100 health care consumerization index combining six measures: convenience expectations, control over treatment, control over costs, viewing health products as consumer goods, preference for online health information, and trust in it.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Index ranks markets by readiness for consumer-led health models — a market-entry screen.

insights.claim: China, India, the UAE and Brazil score highest on BCG's health care consumerization index, likely because their systems are newer, out-of-pocket spending shares are high, and constrained access forces patients to shop actively.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Emerging markets with high out-of-pocket spend are prime for DTC pharma, digital health and private provider growth.

insights.claim: Among established health systems the US is the most consumerized, Western European countries less so given heavier public provision, and Japan — the world's oldest population — is the least consumerized of the ten markets surveyed.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Consumer-health business models travel better to the US than to Europe or Japan.
insights.locator: But patients in nations with more firmly established systems

insights.claim: 45% of US respondents would rather get instant health information from online resources like ChatGPT, Google or WebMD than wait for a professional, versus 40% in Brazil, while 82% of Brazilians want more control over health choices — the highest of any market.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: AI/search is becoming a first-line health channel in the US — a distribution battleground for pharma and providers.
insights.locator: There are, however, some interesting exceptions

insights.claim: Across markets men are slightly more likely than women to rate online medical information as reliable as a professional's (42% vs 38%), while in China women score 9 points higher than men on the consumerization index.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Segment-specific targeting matters; gender gaps are small except in China.

insights.claim: 53% of millennials and 52% of Gen Z view medicines as ordinary consumer goods versus 41% of Gen X and 31% of baby boomers, and 52% of millennials prefer an instant AI or online answer to waiting for a clinician versus 25% of boomers.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Consumerization should deepen structurally as cohorts age in — a secular tailwind for digital health.

insights.claim: BCG finds Gen Z, though digitally fluent, still values human guidance for complex high-stakes decisions, which is why millennials rather than Gen Z lead in preferring instant AI answers.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Pure-AI health models may underperform with the youngest cohort on high-stakes care; hybrid human+AI wins.

insights.claim: 48% of higher-income respondents are willing to pay out of pocket for health products like GLP-1 drugs versus 31% of lower-income respondents, and consumerization rises with income in nearly every market.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Self-pay GLP-1 and wellness demand skews affluent — supports cash-pay channels and premium pricing for that segment.

insights.claim: Self-purchase of health products is driven by payers not covering what patients want, counterintuitive coverage design where self-pay is cheaper than insurance plus copay, and people choosing to self-insure.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Cash-pay pharmacy and DTC channels can undercut insured pricing — a threat to payer gatekeeping and PBM economics.
insights.locator: Different factors drive the trend toward self-purchase

insights.claim: BCG expects biomedical innovation — longevity treatments, multi-biomarker wearables, AI-personalized treatment and AI-enabled care delivery — to keep blurring the line between health care and the cosmetics, lifestyle and fitness industries.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Convergence of health and consumer categories expands TAM for wearables and longevity players.

insights.claim: BCG judges complete consumerization of health care unlikely because most pharmaceuticals and devices will never be widely available without prescription and physicians will retain responsibility for outcomes.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Prescriber relationships remain the core moat for pharma; consumer channels supplement rather than replace them.
insights.quote: although we expect the consumerization of health care to continue, complete consumerization is unlikely
insights.locator: As a result, although we expect

insights.claim: Digital-first care models — AI symptom checkers, app storefronts for therapies, minute-level algorithmic approval — improve access for some but exclude people with low connectivity or health literacy and risk fragmenting care across platforms.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Regulatory and equity backlash is a risk for telehealth/DTC platforms; integrated-record players have an advantage.
insights.locator: Even digital-first models of health care delivery

insights.claim: For biopharma, BCG says consumerization raises the importance of earning patient trust earlier, including making reliable information discoverable via large language models, and rethinking pricing where patients pay directly.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: 'LLM discoverability' becomes a new marketing battleground; direct-pay pricing (e.g., GLP-1 cash channels) spreads.

insights.claim: For medtech, consumerization shifts who chooses and operates the product, emphasizing consumer-grade usability, software and services, new channels and pricing models; for providers it means being found in search and AI results and pairing convenience with clinical continuity.
insights.speaker: Chris Meier
insights.so_what: Favors medtech with software/service revenue and providers investing in digital front doors.
